description: Test your knowledge of Introduction to the nervous system with flashcards covering CNS/PNS organization, autonomic nervous system, neuroglial cells, and neuron structure.

cards.text: What are the three major divisions of the nervous system and where is the CNS located?
cards.answer: CNS: Brain (in cranium) + spinal cord (in vertebral canal); PNS: All nervous tissue outside CNS (cranial/spinal nerves, ganglia); ANS: Part of PNS controlling involuntary visceral functions.

tip.tip: CNS = Central (brain + cord), PNS = Peripheral (outside), ANS = Autonomic (automatic/involuntary)

cards.text: How do sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia locations differ? Which has longer preganglionic fibers?
cards.answer: Sympathetic: Ganglia in paravertebral chains/collateral (near spinal cord) = short preganglionic + long postganglionic. Parasympathetic: Ganglia in/near target organs = long preganglionic + short postganglionic.

tip.tip: Sympathetic goes SHORT-then-LONG (paravertebral start). Parasympathetic goes LONG-then-SHORT (reaches target organ)

cards.text: What is the functional relationship between neurons and neuroglia in the nervous system?
cards.answer: Neurons transmit electrochemical signals (functional units); neuroglia are supporting cells (10× more numerous) that provide structural support, insulation, immunity, and metabolic support.

tip.tip: Neurons = the 'workers' sending signals; glia = the 'support staff' (glue = supportive)

cards.text: Oligodendrocytes vs Schwann cells: How many axons does each myelinate, and where are they found?
cards.answer: Oligodendrocytes (CNS): 1 cell myelinates multiple axons. Schwann cells (PNS): 1 cell myelinates 1 axon segment. Key difference: MS affects oligodendrocytes (CNS demyelination); GBS affects Schwann cells (PNS demyelination).

tip.tip: Oligo = multiple (Greek oligos). Schwann = single. CNS disease = Multiple Sclerosis (many lesions possible). PNS disease = GBS (ascending paralysis).

cards.text: Where are Nissl bodies located in a neuron and what happens to them after axon injury?
cards.answer: Nissl bodies (rough ER + ribosomes) present in: soma, dendrites; ABSENT in axon hillock and axon. After injury: chromatolysis (dissolution/disappearance of Nissl bodies) indicates neuronal stress/degeneration.

tip.tip: Nissl = protein factory. Axon = no factory (can't repair itself well). Injury → chromatolysis (color loss) = cell is stressed.

cards.text: Classify neurons by number of processes and give one CNS example for each type.
cards.answer: Multipolar (many dendrites + 1 axon): anterior horn motor neurons, Purkinje cells. Bipolar (1 dendrite + 1 axon): retinal bipolar cells. Unipolar/pseudounipolar (1 T-shaped process): DRG sensory neurons.

tip.tip: Multi = most common (motor neurons). Bi = rare (retina, vestibular). Uni = sensory ganglia only (DRG). Hint: Most neurons = Multipolar.

cards.text: What is the function of dendritic spines and where do action potentials originate in a neuron?
cards.answer: Dendritic spines: tiny protrusions that increase synaptic surface area for receiving input. Action potential originates at the axon hillock (trigger zone, where impulse is initiated and carried away from soma).

tip.tip: Spines = increase surface = better reception. Axon hillock = 'trigger' zone (where spike starts). Flow: dendrites → soma → AH → axon → terminal.

cards.text: Which neuroglia cell is responsible for myelination in the CNS, and what glioma arises from astrocytes?
cards.answer: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons. Astrocytes are prone to glioma formation: astrocytoma and glioblastoma are the most common primary brain tumours.

tip.tip: Oligo = CNS myelin. Astro = star-shaped, forms tumours (glio-BLASTOMA = worst grade). Remember: Oligo myelin, Astro tumours.
